transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-02-14 15:30 UTC
Duration: 64 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jorge (Redwood SE), Maya (Neptune), Carlos (Neptune), Lena (Neptune), Tom (Neptune)

Summary: Quick demo/playthrough focusing on edge behaviors: very long context windows (~200k tokens simulated), sustained high TPS with burst patterns, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. Showed Redwood Console telemetry, Optimize recommendations, and fallback routing from hosted -> dedicated variants. Agreed to run a larger stress test in the sandbox and share security docs.

Topics: long context preservation, KV/prefix cache eviction, batching windows and micro-batching, streaming chunked transfer and SSE vs websocket behavior, request timeouts and graceful fallback, routing to quantized model variants, autoscale and burst capacity, observability in Console, cost tradeoffs.

-- Transcript Body --
[15:30] Alex Moore: okay everybody thanks for joining, we'll run through an edge playthrough today, focus on long context and high throughput streaming backpressure. if anything's unclear just interrupt.
[15:31] Maya Chen: sounds good, we have lena and carlos here who are very focused on the SRE side; our main worry is long running sessions eating memory and then streaming stalling — we've seen other vendors drop the stream at like 30 seconds.
[15:31] Priya Singh: right. we've seen that pattern a lot; i'll walk through kv cache strategies and our graceful fallback. quick note — our default http idle timeout is 60s on hosted but you can extend with request_timeout param for streaming sessions.
[15:32] Carlos Ruiz: is that per request or per socket? sometimes our gateway closes sockets at 45s because of a load-balancer.
[15:32] Priya Singh: it's per request. but we recommend coordinating with LB timeouts; for streaming we suggest use of websockets or server-sent events (SSE) with keepalive pings. if you have strict LB limits, you can set chunk flush intervals shorter so the LB sees activity.
[15:33] Lena Park: have you seen issues with chunked transfer on some corporate LBs? they sometimes buffer and then send big bursts.
[15:33] Jorge Alvarez: yes, buffering happens; chunked transfer encoding sometimes is invisibly re-buffered by intermediaries. Our console shows rebuffer counts under streaming diagnostics so you can correlate.
[15:34] Tom Whitby: from product POV we want user-visible progress even under heavy load; falling back gracefully to a shorter model is okay as long as we get partial answers.
[15:34] Alex Moore: exactly — that's where our routing policies come in: you can prioritize latency SLO and route to a faster quantized variant or enable a degrade-to-summary policy. i'll demo that.
[15:35] Priya Singh: starting demo: first i'm simulating long-context sessions — think 150k to 250k tokens — by stitching previous interactions and using prefix caching. watch the KV cache hit rate in Console.
[15:36] [15:36] Priya Singh: (screen share) Console -> Models -> Session telemetry: you can see our KV cache growth, per-session memory footprint, and when eviction happens. notice the eviction threshold triggers at around 22GB per GPU in this config and it evicts oldest prefix entries.
[15:37] Maya Chen: can we pin sessions to avoid eviction for VIP users?
[15:37] Priya Singh: yes — Dedicated can reserve memory pools per-tenant and pin hot sessions. hosted has soft-pinning plus autoscaling but for absolute guarantees you go Dedicated.
[15:38] Carlos Ruiz: how is the latency impacted when eviction occurs and you have to rehydrate KV from cold storage?
[15:38] Priya Singh: rehydrate means you either fetch from prefix cache in an external cache (we support Redis or our managed prefix-store) — that adds ~50-200ms depending on network. if we fall back to recompute from scratch, the delta can be seconds. so the big recommendation is keep a small working set cached and use selective truncation.
[15:39] Jorge Alvarez: side note — Optimize will analyze your session histograms and recommend the quantization profile and cache TTLs per route. in the demo i've enabled Optimize suggestions for this workload: it recommends micro-batching at 20ms windows for 8k TPS bursts to hit the 95th percentile latency target.
[15:40] [15:40] Priya Singh: switching to high TPS sim — i'm firing a mixed load: 70% short queries, 30% long-context streaming with incremental deltas. watch the request queue length and stream backpressure metric.
[15:41] [15:41] (sim running)
[15:41] Maya Chen: we're seeing queues spike to 900 requests in the sim — how do we avoid that?
[15:41] Priya Singh: that's queue saturation; options: increase batching concurrency, add dedicated capacity, or enable our graceful-shed policy that rejects the tail and returns early summary tokens. another lever is KV cache warming and sticky routing so long-sessions hit the same shard.
[15:42] Lena Park: graceful-shed policy — does that do partial responses, or HTTP 429?
[15:42] Priya Singh: configurable. you can return a 200 with a partial summary and a flag like "partial=true, truncated=true" so clients can show partial content and optionally retry. or you can reject with 429 along with a recommended backoff.
[15:43] Carlos Ruiz: what's the default behavior on hosted?
[15:43] Alex Moore: hosted defaults to keeping latency SLO and will route to a cheaper variant if throughput spikes and latency would break. it prefers return partial data over hard errors, but you can flip policy.
[15:44] [15:44] (Console view) Queue depth graph shows a sawtooth with periodic backpressure spikes. Priya toggles fallback routing.
[15:45] Priya Singh: i just triggered automatic fallback: long streaming sessions were switched to a faster 8-bit quantized model. note token quality drop is minor for summarization use-cases. i also switched to shorter chunk flush (150ms) to keep LB alive.
[15:46] Tom Whitby: how do we measure quality regressions when fallback happens? we need a guardrail.
[15:46] Priya Singh: Optimize ties regression alerts to your evaluation set; you can instrument a small prompt bank that runs every minute, and if ROUGE/BLEU/semantic-similarity drops beyond threshold, it will alert and optionally block automatic fallback.
[15:47] Maya Chen: can those evals run in parallel to production without adding cost?
[15:47] Priya Singh: they run in a low-cost monitor pool; cost is minimal because you can use a smaller model for evaluation but still get signal.
[15:48] Carlos Ruiz: let's talk timeouts again — in our infra the gateway kills long TCPs at 45s, but the request body may keep sending chunks after that. how does Redwood handle mid-stream disconnects?
[15:48] Priya Singh: we checkpoint the KV cache at configurable intervals. if the client reconnects within the session TTL, we can resume from last checkpoint. session TTLs can be tuned; default is 24h for hosted but you can shorten/lengthen.
[15:49] Lena Park: sounds good. what about TLS termination and KMS — we need to ensure keys never leave our HSM.
[15:49] Jorge Alvarez: Private deployments support customer-managed KMS and HSM. for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with BYOK support on Dedicated or Private. we'll share the SOC2+HSM note.
[15:50] [15:50] (Sim shows a disconnect)
[15:50] Priya Singh: when a disconnect occurs you'll see a "stream interrupted" event and Console will automatically show replays per session. we also surface cause: LB closed, app closed, or server OOM.
[15:51] Maya Chen: in the sim we saw a few stream resets correlated with GC pauses on the worker VMs — is that something you control?
[15:51] Priya Singh: GC on customer VMs would be a factor for Private deployments; for Hosted our runtime uses controlled memory alloc patterns and we pin allocs to avoid OS-level GC pauses. we can provide deeper traces.
[15:52] Tom Whitby: about cost — how much more expensive is Dedicated for pinned memory vs hosted autoscale?
[15:52] Alex Moore: Dedicated is premium — it's predictable and higher baseline. cost delta depends on utilization; if you're constantly at high sustained concurrency, Dedicated is typically cheaper per-token. We can model this in the spreadsheet.
[15:53] Carlos Ruiz: okay next, show the observability -> what we get for root cause.
[15:53] Priya Singh: Console: per-token latency, per-session KV size, evicted prefixes, streaming rebuffer count, fallback events, and per-model quality delta. here i'm filtering to our test route and showing the event timeline with correlated infra metrics.
[15:54] [15:54] (Priya points to event annotatoins) some of the spikes correlate with autoscaler throttles due to VCPU limits.
[15:55] Alex Moore: final part — run a live fallback: i'll flip the policy to degrade to a summarizer model under >500 queue depth and show the client experience.
[15:56] [15:56] (client view) user sees progressive updates, then a final "partial" flag with a link to full content queued for async generation.
[15:57] Maya Chen: ok that's acceptable for our knowledge retrieval flows. for billing will partial answers still count as full tokens?
[15:57] Alex Moore: billing is per-token generated. partial answers are billed for the tokens produced; if you later request a full re-run, that is billed separately unless you use an async rerun that dedups cached prefixes.
[15:58] Lena Park: any recommended client-side patterns?
[15:58] Priya Singh: yes — implement idempotent request IDs, incremental rendering on the client, and an exponential backoff with jitter for retries. also surface the "partial" flag and offer the user the option to wait for full run.
[15:59] [15:59] (wrap-up)
[16:00] Alex Moore: recap — we'll run the 1h 10k TPS mixed workload in your sandbox, share the stress spreadsheet and console exports, and provide security pack. next meeting to review results week of 2027-02-22.
[16:01] Carlos Ruiz: thanks all, please include the KMS/HSM note and a short FAQ on timeouts and LB coordination.
[16:02] Maya Chen: thanks — appreciate the demo.

End of transcript.
